angular-frequency-from-complex-frequency.title: Angular Frequency as the Imaginary Part of Complex Frequency
angular-frequency-from-complex-frequency.description: This definitional relationship identifies the angular frequency $\omega$ of an oscillatory system with the imaginary part of its complex frequency $\sigma$.
angular-frequency-from-complex-frequency.conceptual_definition: In the analysis of linear systems, solutions often take the exponential form $A(t) = A_0 e^{\sigma t}$, where $\sigma$ is the complex frequency. By expressing $\sigma$ in terms of its real and imaginary parts, $\sigma = \gamma + i\omega$, the time evolution becomes $A(t) = A_0 e^{\gamma t} e^{i\omega t}$. The term $e^{\gamma t}$ governs the amplitude's exponential growth ($\gamma > 0$) or decay ($\gamma < 0$). The term $e^{i\omega t}$, by Euler's formula, represents pure oscillation with angular frequency $\omega$. This equation, $\omega = \text{Im}(\sigma)$, is the formal definition that isolates this oscillatory component.
angular-frequency-from-complex-frequency.interpretation: The complex frequency $\sigma$ provides a complete description of the temporal evolution of a single mode in a linear system. Its real part, $\gamma = \text{Re}(\sigma)$, is the damping rate (if $\gamma < 0$) or growth rate (if $\gamma > 0$). Its imaginary part, $\omega = \text{Im}(\sigma)$, is the angular frequency of oscillation. This equation, $\omega = \text{Im}(\sigma)$, is a definitional identity that separates the oscillatory behavior from the amplitude change. For a system to oscillate, it must have a non-zero imaginary part in its characteristic complex frequency, i.e., $\omega \neq 0$. The period of oscillation is then given by $T = 2\pi/\omega$.
angular-frequency-from-complex-frequency.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where $\text{Im}(\sigma) \to 0$, the angular frequency $\omega \to 0$, and the system exhibits no oscillatory behavior; its evolution is pure exponential decay or growth, governed by $\text{Re}(\sigma)$. Conversely, in the case of marginal stability where $\text{Re}(\sigma) = 0$, the system experiences pure, undamped oscillation at the frequency $\omega = \text{Im}(\sigma)$. If both $\text{Re}(\sigma) = 0$ and $\text{Im}(\sigma) = 0$, the system is static.
angular-frequency-from-complex-frequency.symmetry_origin: This relationship is not derived from a fundamental physical symmetry via Noether's theorem. Instead, it is a definitional consequence of using complex exponential functions, $e^{\sigma t}$, as basis solutions for linear differential equations that are invariant under time translation. The mathematical structure of complex numbers naturally separates the solution into an exponential amplitude part and an oscillatory phase part.

x-component-of-curl-of-gradient-2764c704.title: X-Component of the Curl of a Gradient Field
x-component-of-curl-of-gradient-2764c704.description: This identity demonstrates that the x-component of the curl of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$, where $\mathbf{F}$ is the gradient of a scalar potential $\psi$, is identically zero due to the commutativity of partial derivatives.
x-component-of-curl-of-gradient-2764c704.conceptual_definition: The x-component of the curl of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ is defined as $(\nabla \times \mathbf{F})_x = \frac{\partial F_z}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial F_y}{\partial z}$. If the field $\mathbf{F}$ is conservative, it can be expressed as the gradient of a scalar potential, $\mathbf{F} = \nabla \psi$. Substituting the components of the gradient, $F_y = \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}$ and $F_z = \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial z}$, into the definition of the curl's x-component yields $\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial z}\right) - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}\right)$. By Clairaut's theorem on the equality of mixed partials, this expression is identically zero for any sufficiently smooth scalar function $\psi$.

It is not subject to physical limits such as temperature $T \to 0$ or velocity $v \to c$. It is a fundamental property of vector calculus in a flat, three-dimensional Euclidean space.
x-component-of-curl-of-gradient-2764c704.symmetry_origin: Geometric identity of Euclidean space; it relies on the commutativity of partial derivatives (Clairaut's theorem), which holds for sufficiently smooth scalar fields defined on a manifold.
